Ways To Pass A Drug Test

Passing A Drug Test

An Introduction to the VCL
By Michael D. Cutler

March 1, 1998

The Problem: The Drug War drones on, consuming precious public funds to incarcerate primarily non-violent minority drug users (rarely the drug lords who acquire most drug profit), with little tax money available for public drug treatment and no impact on the availability of drugs to children. When more voters learn the truth about the financial irresponsibility of the Drug War, however, the war will end as taxpayers demand that the same dollars used to incarcerate one drug user, be used instead to treat ten for abuse as outpatients.

The public never hears the truth, however, because (among other reasons) government and private business fear mongers demonize anyone criticizing our current drug policy as "legalizers" who encourage drug abuse. The drug war’s failure unfortunately generates more fear of drugs than the courage to implement a better system of controls. Thus, part of the solution to ending the Drug War, is providing the public with responsible, accurate information about the Drug War and its consequences.

The Lesson of Alcohol Prohibition. This disconnection now occurring in Drug War ideology, between government policy directed at protecting people from self abuse, and the facts, has a direct and compelling historical precedent: Alcohol Prohibition. Prohibition produced the same result as seen today, in funding criminal cartels of alcohol suppliers, rising levels of violence between competing gangs and the police, the proliferation of dangerously adulterated and more powerful intoxicants, corrupting police with prohibition-driven profits and swelling prisons with non-violent retail alcohol distributors, while the wholesalers bought their way out of prosecution.

Demonizing Dissent. Prohibition opposition began to grow in the first decade following the imposition of Prohibition, as the harm it created grew to far outweigh the perceived benefits that making alcohol illegal was designed to achieve. Legislators were locked into Prohibition, however, by the refusal of polite society to reconsider the wisdom of attempting to control by criminal sanction the human desire for intoxication. Any breach in the crusade to jail alcohol distributors was deemed sacrilegious and worthy of social and political condemnation.

Attorneys Left to Clean Up Prohibition’s Mess. One group saw the damaging impact of Prohibition vividly, because it so cluttered their places of business and the businesses of their customers. That group was the attorneys, who saw daily the clogging of court business with Prohibition enforcement, the corruption of the police attempting such enforcement and the growth of criminal business from bootlegging profits, threatening the safety of their legitimate business clients. Attorneys, perhaps more so then than now, also held their communities’ respect as advisers to the captains of industry and government. They also felt compelled to react to the corrosion of civil liberties and growing public disrespect for the criminal justice system, being caused by Prohibition.

Legalizing Discourse. In 1927, nine prominent but pragmatic lawyers decided to take on the social damage of Prohibition, suffered by growing numbers of businesses, clients and fellow citizens. Their objective was to organize local bar associations to study the effects of Prohibition, publish the results and lobby local politicians to legislate any changes the studies might recommend. They called themselves the Voluntary Committee of Lawyers (VCL), headquartered in New York City. By 1932, the organization had more than 3000 members in every state of the union. Their primary role, in promoting bar association investigations of Prohibition, was simple: To bring a consideration of the merits of Prohibition into "polite society," to enable mainstream discussion about whether Prohibition was serving the national interest, without dissent being demonized as somehow encouraging alcoholism.

Attorneys Find Common Ground. Lawyers, seeing the deteriorating impact of Prohibition in courtrooms throughout the country, quickly reached a broad consensus that Prohibition had failed, and was causing more harm than alcoholism had before the liquor ban. Although initially a northeastern venture, western state bar associations and the city bar groups in many southern cities quickly found Prohibition untenable in their local districts, and joined the repeal cause under the leadership of the VCL.

As the Debate Grew, Public Opinion Changed. As bar reports recommending repeal proliferated, the more common in public debate became questions about the Prohibition’s ability to achieve national sobriety, and over the afford-ability of the costs of attempting more vigorous Prohibition enforcement. Lawyers alone did not convince the public, but lawyers helped foster a public willingness to consider the prospect of replacing Prohibition with a better policy. Once the debate began, the public consensus for repeal began to grow inexorably.

Implementing Prohibition Repeal. As popular opinion shifted toward Prohibition Repeal, the VCL moved from bar associations to the state and federal legislatures and national party conventions. VCL members drafted the repeal plank of the 1932 Democratic Convention that elected Franklin Roosevelt, beginning with the (now familiar) enumeration of Prohibition problems:

"Whereas, the direct results of attempted enforcement have been to imperil the liberties of the people, to finance organized crime, to plunge politics in corruption, to clog the courts of justice, to fill the prisons, and to subject important communities to a rule of conduct which they disapprove and strenuously resist, so that large sections of the electorate have come to regard the Federal Government as a hostile and alien power";

VCL attorneys also drafted proposals for statutes in virtually all states for controlling alcohol distribution after repeal of prohibition, and a new federal alcohol control law. The final work of the VCL involved the elaboration of the repeal process itself, as Prohibition had been made an amendment to the federal constitution when adopted. The VCL repeal coordination was national in scope and meteoric in its implementation and success. From federal enabling legislation to the 36th state’s endorsement of repeal, the constitutional re-amendment process took only nine months.

The New VCL. Less than two years ago, a new collection of prominent lawyers looked at the Drug War and saw lessons for its repair in Alcohol Prohibition and the activities of the original VCL. Northampton Mass. attorney Richard Evans brought the historical records of the VCL to the attention of a NY drug policy group, the Partnership for Responsible Drug Information.

Using Evans’ work, the PRDI helped assemble a new VCL founding board, including such luminaries as two former US Attorney Generals, Massachusetts’ own Elliot Richardson and Nicholas Katzenbach, Pres. Johnson’s AG and later chief corporate counsel for IBM. Other founders include Leon Higginbotham, retired chief justice of the third federal circuit court of appeals now at Harvard’s Kennedy School of Government; George Bushnell, former ABA Pres.; NY labor mediator Ted Kheel; and Samuel Dash, Georgetown Law Prof. and chief legal counsel to the Judiciary Committee of the US Senate under NC Sen. Sam Ervin, who conducted the Watergate investigation (he remains minority counsel to the committee).

The modern VCL is a non-profit corporation, currently based in NYC, devoted to encouraging the legal community to carefully consider the "War on Drugs" and the relative benefits of alternate policies. Lawyers have the skill and training to evaluate these approaches without prejudging them, and assess which methods may work better. These options include innovative treatment and "harm reduction" programs developed in America and in Europe.

Other alternatives to be explored include decriminalization of adult marijuana use and cultivation, greater freedom for physicians to prescribe illicit drugs, scientific and medical research (now prohibited) on illicit drug effects, drug education based on scientific fact rather than fear and moral posturing, and a reconstruction of the eroding state and federal constitutional protections against government invasion of citizen privacy. Many of these alternative policies require only a shift in administrative and budget priorities. Others require well-crafted changes in local, state, and federal statutes.

The modern VCL pursues two broad programs:

Protection for Dissent. First, the VCL encourages bar associations across the United States to investigate the consequences of the current drug laws. Every bar association "Committee on Drugs and the Law," that has investigated these laws in the past five years, has advocated major reforms in the criminal enforcement basis of our current drug policy. As attorneys address the subject, they become better informed and able to communicate responsible information to the public. The VCL thus works to create a zone of political comfort, where fellow professionals (and ultimately, legislators) can reveal misgivings about the war without being condemned as "pro-drug."

How to Adopt a Better Drug Policy. Second, the VCL provides model statutes to control drugs and implement alternative drug policies. The drug war’s roots into our legal landscape have grown deeply over the past 60 years, but they can be carefully removed without damaging our surrounding legal foundation. Reform efforts must solve conflicts between state and federal law. Model drug laws must integrate administrative law, employment law, family law and pharmaceutical regulation, as well as criminal justice and prison administration. By developing model legislation, the VCL helps reduce the fear of changing current drug policy by providing a structured vision of future control regulation.

The Work of the New VCL. Early projects of the new VCL included a public drug policy forum, sponsored by the Waterbury (CT) Bar Association last year. It featured a number of prominent CT attorneys, state legislators, government and academic public health specialists, doctors, judges and prosecutors among the panelists and observers. The keynote speaker was former U.S. Atty. Gen. Katzenbach, a VCL Founder.

A second forum, entitled "Is the Drug War Forever?" was held at Suffolk University in Boston in January 1998, produced by Richard Evans and your author of this article. Although scheduled keynoter, VCL co-founder, former AG and Ambassador Elliot Richardson canceled due to family illness, he was replaced by moderator Anthony Lewis of the NY Times, twice honored with journalism’s Pulitzer Prize.

The Boston Panelists. Panel presentations were made by Northeastern Univ. Law Prof. John Flym, discussing the racially-oriented history of federal drug laws; Hon. Nancy Gertner, a judge of Boston’s federal trial court, discussing the unjust impact of federal mandatory minimum sentencing law on the least blameworthy members of drug distribution schemes; and, Dr. David Lewis of Brown University, who described the creation of a national doctor’s group (Physicians’ Leadership for National Drug Policy), empowered to dispassionately investigate the Drug War and publicize its conclusions in much the same manner as the VCL’s work with lawyers.

VCL Plans. The future of the VCL is encouraging. Several public drug policy forums have been held in New York City and Minneapolis. Interest in supporting similar programs exists throughout the country; the VCL is in touch with potential forum producing attorneys in Seattle, Oakland, Denver, Chicago, Detroit, New Orleans, Tallahassee, Albequerque, Philadelphia, Hawaii, Oregon and Virginia. The VCL has an Internet site (www.vcl.org). A major foundation has approached the VCL about funding, as has a nationally-oriented law school about providing the organization a formal headquarters. VCL activity helps demonstrate the mainstream nature of dissent to the Drug War, and serves to demonstrate before an increasingly interested electorate, the transparent futility of the Drug War.
